value.misconception: IP guarantees packets arrive exactly once and in order.
value.correction: IP is best-effort and connectionless; loss, duplication, corruption and reordering are possible.

value.misconception: IP and TCP are the same protocol.
value.correction: IP is network layer; TCP is transport layer and connection-oriented.

value.misconception: An IP datagram and Ethernet frame are the same unit.
value.correction: The IP datagram is encapsulated inside a link-layer frame.

value.misconception: Routers always notify endpoints when they discard packets.
value.correction: ICMP may report errors, but router notification is not required for every error.

value.misconception: IPv6 routers fragment packets like IPv4 routers.
value.correction: IPv6 network elements do not fragment; endpoints must respect Path MTU.

value.misconception: IPv6 has the same IP header checksum as IPv4.
value.correction: IPv4 has a header checksum; IPv6 omits it under the source-stated assumption.

value.misconception: If a packet fits the local MTU, it fits the whole path.
value.correction: Path MTU can be smaller because another link may impose a tighter limit.

value.misconception: Multicast and broadcast both reach every node.
value.correction: Broadcast reaches all nodes in scope; multicast reaches a selected group.

value.misconception: Anycast always chooses the geographically closest machine.
value.correction: The source describes a distance or cost measure, not necessarily geography.

value.misconception: IPv5 was the deployed successor to IPv4.
value.correction: Version 5 was used by experimental Internet Stream Protocol.

value.misconception: Every IP version number is a deployed standard.
value.correction: The version list includes experimental, obsolete, reserved, unassigned and joke/proposal entries.

value.misconception: IP alone guarantees confidentiality and security.
value.correction: The source notes vulnerabilities and names IPsec; it does not claim IP itself guarantees confidentiality.

value.misconception: TCP and UDP adapt to MTU identically.
value.correction: TCP adjusts segment size; oversized UDP/ICMP may trigger IP fragmentation.

value.misconception: The source details NIC ASIC, CPU and RAM-buffer architecture.
value.correction: The article explicitly names routers and Layer 3 switches; other hardware details are synthesis.

value.misconception: Every packet to a destination takes the same path.
value.correction: Datagrams are routed independently and may take different paths.

value.misconception: The IP header is the application data.
value.correction: Header carries addressing/metadata; payload carries transported data.

value.misconception: OSI Layer 3 and the TCP/IP Internet layer are unrelated.
value.correction: The article maps IP to OSI network layer and TCP/IP Internet layer.

value.misconception: Broadcast reaches every Internet host.
value.correction: Broadcast scope is generally a network subnet.

value.misconception: IPv6 immediately replaced IPv4.
value.correction: The article describes a gradual increase in IPv6 deployment since around 2006.

value.misconception: Link-layer error detection eliminates end-to-end reliability needs.
value.correction: Endpoint and upper-layer compensation remains part of the described design.

value.misconception: Link capacity and MTU mean the same thing.
value.correction: Capacity is transmission rate; MTU is maximum packet size.

value.misconception: Anycast sends to every member of a group.
value.correction: Anycast selects one receiver; multicast can send to a group.

value.misconception: Routing protocols carry user payload instead of IP.
value.correction: Routing protocols exchange route information; IP forwarding carries datagrams.

value.misconception: IPv4 header checksum verifies all payload end-to-end.
value.correction: The source says it safeguards the IPv4 header, not end-to-end payload integrity.

value.misconception: All routers use the same CPU/ASIC architecture.
value.correction: Implementation varies; CPU/ASIC mapping is explanatory, not universal.

value.misconception: IP fragmentation is always preferred for TCP.
value.correction: TCP adjusts segment size to fit MTU in the source description.

value.misconception: Dynamic routing guarantees ordered delivery.
value.correction: Different paths can cause out-of-order delivery; hosts/upper layers may buffer.

value.misconception: All graph hardware extensions are externally verified.
value.correction: No external research was used; extensions are labeled synthesis/expansion.

misconceptions.misconception: IP guarantees packets arrive exactly once and in order.
misconceptions.correction: IP is best-effort and connectionless; loss, duplication, corruption and reordering are possible.

misconceptions.misconception: IP and TCP are the same protocol.
misconceptions.correction: IP is network layer; TCP is transport layer and connection-oriented.

misconceptions.misconception: An IP datagram and Ethernet frame are the same unit.
misconceptions.correction: The IP datagram is encapsulated inside a link-layer frame.

misconceptions.misconception: Routers always notify endpoints when they discard packets.
misconceptions.correction: ICMP may report errors, but router notification is not required for every error.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv6 routers fragment packets like IPv4 routers.
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 network elements do not fragment; endpoints must respect Path MTU.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv6 has the same IP header checksum as IPv4.
misconceptions.correction: IPv4 has a header checksum; IPv6 omits it under the source-stated assumption.

misconceptions.misconception: If a packet fits the local MTU, it fits the whole path.
misconceptions.correction: Path MTU can be smaller because another link may impose a tighter limit.

misconceptions.misconception: Multicast and broadcast both reach every node.
misconceptions.correction: Broadcast reaches all nodes in scope; multicast reaches a selected group.

misconceptions.misconception: Anycast always chooses the geographically closest machine.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes a distance or cost measure, not necessarily geography.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv5 was the deployed successor to IPv4.
misconceptions.correction: Version 5 was used by experimental Internet Stream Protocol.

misconceptions.misconception: Every IP version number is a deployed standard.
misconceptions.correction: The version list includes experimental, obsolete, reserved, unassigned and joke/proposal entries.

misconceptions.misconception: IP alone guarantees confidentiality and security.
misconceptions.correction: The source notes vulnerabilities and names IPsec; it does not claim IP itself guarantees confidentiality.

misconceptions.misconception: TCP and UDP adapt to MTU identically.
misconceptions.correction: TCP adjusts segment size; oversized UDP/ICMP may trigger IP fragmentation.

misconceptions.misconception: The source details NIC ASIC, CPU and RAM-buffer architecture.
misconceptions.correction: The article explicitly names routers and Layer 3 switches; other hardware details are synthesis.

misconceptions.misconception: Every packet to a destination takes the same path.
misconceptions.correction: Datagrams are routed independently and may take different paths.

misconceptions.misconception: The IP header is the application data.
misconceptions.correction: Header carries addressing/metadata; payload carries transported data.

misconceptions.misconception: OSI Layer 3 and the TCP/IP Internet layer are unrelated.
misconceptions.correction: The article maps IP to OSI network layer and TCP/IP Internet layer.

misconceptions.misconception: Broadcast reaches every Internet host.
misconceptions.correction: Broadcast scope is generally a network subnet.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv6 immediately replaced IPv4.
misconceptions.correction: The article describes a gradual increase in IPv6 deployment since around 2006.

misconceptions.misconception: Link-layer error detection eliminates end-to-end reliability needs.
misconceptions.correction: Endpoint and upper-layer compensation remains part of the described design.

misconceptions.misconception: Link capacity and MTU mean the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Capacity is transmission rate; MTU is maximum packet size.

misconceptions.misconception: Anycast sends to every member of a group.
misconceptions.correction: Anycast selects one receiver; multicast can send to a group.

misconceptions.misconception: Routing protocols carry user payload instead of IP.
misconceptions.correction: Routing protocols exchange route information; IP forwarding carries datagrams.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv4 header checksum verifies all payload end-to-end.
misconceptions.correction: The source says it safeguards the IPv4 header, not end-to-end payload integrity.

misconceptions.misconception: All routers use the same CPU/ASIC architecture.
misconceptions.correction: Implementation varies; CPU/ASIC mapping is explanatory, not universal.

misconceptions.misconception: IP fragmentation is always preferred for TCP.
misconceptions.correction: TCP adjusts segment size to fit MTU in the source description.

misconceptions.misconception: Dynamic routing guarantees ordered delivery.
misconceptions.correction: Different paths can cause out-of-order delivery; hosts/upper layers may buffer.

misconceptions.misconception: All graph hardware extensions are externally verified.
misconceptions.correction: No external research was used; extensions are labeled synthesis/expansion.

value.label: No IPv6 broadcast
value.description: IPv6 has no broadcast address; all-nodes multicast is used for the analogous attached-link function.

value.label: IPv6 vs IPv4
value.description: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses and a different packet/header model; IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses and its own packet format.

value.label: Unicast vs anycast vs multicast
value.description: IPv6 defines all three transmission/addressing modes with different destination semantics.

value.label: Multicast vs broadcast
value.description: IPv6 has no broadcast; all-nodes multicast supplies the analogous attached-link all-host function.

value.label: SLAAC vs DHCPv6
value.description: SLAAC is stateless host/router-based prefix configuration; DHCPv6 can supply additional stateful addresses or information.

value.label: Link-local vs global unicast
value.description: Link-local addresses are local-link and required on IPv6 interfaces; global unicast addresses are globally routable.

value.label: Base header vs extension headers
value.description: The base header is fixed at 40 octets; optional functions are moved to extension headers.

value.label: Router fragmentation vs endpoint fragmentation
value.description: IPv6 routers do not fragment; endpoints can fragment and hosts can use PMTU discovery.

value.label: IPv6 no header checksum vs IPv4 checksum
value.description: IPv6 omits the base-header checksum, unlike IPv4, reducing router recalculation work.

value.label: Dual-stack vs tunneling
value.description: Dual-stack runs both stacks natively; tunneling encapsulates one protocol within another network.

value.label: IPv4-mapped vs IPv4-compatible
value.description: IPv4-mapped addresses remain a hybrid representation; IPv4-compatible addresses are deprecated.

value.label: Stable vs temporary addresses
value.description: Stable/global identifiers support reachability but can facilitate tracking; temporary addresses reduce persistence.

value.label: AAAA vs A DNS records
value.description: AAAA resolves IPv6; A resolves IPv4.

value.label: PMTU discovery vs fragmentation
value.description: PMTU discovery sizes packets for the path; fragmentation is endpoint-only when needed.

value.label: IPsec vs higher-layer security
value.description: The source discusses IPsec at the IP layer but does not equate it with TLS; both occupy different architectural positions.

value.label: Native vs tunneled IPv6
value.description: Native IPv6 traverses IPv6-capable infrastructure; tunneling carries IPv6 over IPv4 infrastructure.

value.title: IPv6 is just IPv4 with bigger addresses
value.correction: IPv6 changes packet format, address architecture, fragmentation behavior, neighbor discovery, multicast/broadcast semantics and other protocol functions.

value.title: IPv6 supports broadcast
value.correction: IPv6 does not define traditional broadcast addresses; multicast is used instead.

value.title: Routers fragment IPv6 packets
value.correction: IPv6 routers do not fragment; hosts use PMTU discovery or endpoint fragmentation.

value.title: IPv6 addresses always need DHCP
value.correction: IPv6 supports SLAAC and hosts generate link-local addresses automatically; DHCPv6 is optional for additional state.

value.title: Every IPv6 address is globally routable
value.correction: IPv6 interfaces require link-local addressing and may have multiple address types; global unicast is only one category.

value.title: IPv6 cannot be scanned
value.correction: The source explicitly notes that configuration patterns can make scanning feasible in real-world scenarios.

value.title: IPv6 has a header checksum like IPv4
value.correction: IPv6 omits the base-header checksum.

value.title: IPv6 and IPv4 interoperate directly
value.correction: The source states the protocols are not directly interoperable and require transition mechanisms.

value.title: IPv6 extension headers are always harmless to routers
value.correction: Some implementations process extension headers in software/CPU paths, causing performance or security issues.

value.title: Global IPv6 addressing eliminates privacy concerns
value.correction: Stable globally addressable identifiers can facilitate tracking; temporary addresses mitigate this concern.

value.title: Tunneling is equivalent to native IPv6
value.correction: Tunneling adds encapsulation and can reduce MTU/increase latency.

value.title: NDP is just ARP with a new address format
value.correction: NDP uses ICMPv6 and multicast and also handles router discovery and address configuration.

value.title: AAAA records are IPv4 DNS records
value.correction: AAAA records map names to IPv6 addresses; A records map names to IPv4.

value.title: IPv6 deployment means IPv4 disappears immediately
value.correction: The source describes coexistence and transition mechanisms because both protocols operate simultaneously.

value.title: IPv6 security is automatically stronger because of the larger address space
value.correction: The source identifies implementation and operational security risks, including shadow networks and fragmentation evasion.

source_claims.claim: IPv6 hosts create link-local addresses and can configure global addresses using router advertisements and SLAAC.

source_claims.title: Neighbor discovery
source_claims.claim: NDP replaces the IPv4 ARP role using ICMPv6 and multicast.

source_claims.title: Packet structure
source_claims.claim: IPv6 packets have a 40-octet base header plus optional extension headers and payload.

source_claims.title: Router fragmentation
source_claims.claim: IPv6 routers do not fragment; hosts use PMTU discovery or endpoint fragmentation.

source_claims.title: DNS integration
source_claims.claim: AAAA records provide IPv6 DNS resolution and ip6.arpa supports reverse resolution.

source_claims.title: Transition
source_claims.claim: Dual-stack and tunneling allow IPv4/IPv6 coexistence; NAT64 provides translation mechanisms.

source_claims.title: Security
source_claims.claim: IPv6 security includes IPsec support but also shadow-network and fragmentation-evasion risks.

source_claims.title: Standardization
source_claims.claim: IPv6 evolved from IPng through RFC 1883, RFC 2460 and RFC 8200.

source_claims.title: Deployment
source_claims.claim: IPv6 deployment has expanded through ISPs, operating systems, mobile networks and Internet services, with the source citing 2026 adoption measurements.

semantic_distinctions.label: No IPv6 broadcast
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv6 has no broadcast address; all-nodes multicast is used for the analogous attached-link function.

semantic_distinctions.label: IPv6 vs IPv4
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses and a different packet/header model; IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses and its own packet format.

semantic_distinctions.label: Unicast vs anycast vs multicast
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv6 defines all three transmission/addressing modes with different destination semantics.

semantic_distinctions.label: Multicast vs broadcast
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv6 has no broadcast; all-nodes multicast supplies the analogous attached-link all-host function.

semantic_distinctions.label: SLAAC vs DHCPv6
semantic_distinctions.description: SLAAC is stateless host/router-based prefix configuration; DHCPv6 can supply additional stateful addresses or information.

semantic_distinctions.label: Link-local vs global unicast
semantic_distinctions.description: Link-local addresses are local-link and required on IPv6 interfaces; global unicast addresses are globally routable.

semantic_distinctions.label: Base header vs extension headers
semantic_distinctions.description: The base header is fixed at 40 octets; optional functions are moved to extension headers.

semantic_distinctions.label: Router fragmentation vs endpoint fragmentation
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv6 routers do not fragment; endpoints can fragment and hosts can use PMTU discovery.

semantic_distinctions.label: IPv6 no header checksum vs IPv4 checksum
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv6 omits the base-header checksum, unlike IPv4, reducing router recalculation work.

semantic_distinctions.label: Dual-stack vs tunneling
semantic_distinctions.description: Dual-stack runs both stacks natively; tunneling encapsulates one protocol within another network.

semantic_distinctions.label: IPv4-mapped vs IPv4-compatible
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv4-mapped addresses remain a hybrid representation; IPv4-compatible addresses are deprecated.

semantic_distinctions.label: Stable vs temporary addresses
semantic_distinctions.description: Stable/global identifiers support reachability but can facilitate tracking; temporary addresses reduce persistence.

semantic_distinctions.label: AAAA vs A DNS records
semantic_distinctions.description: AAAA resolves IPv6; A resolves IPv4.

semantic_distinctions.label: PMTU discovery vs fragmentation
semantic_distinctions.description: PMTU discovery sizes packets for the path; fragmentation is endpoint-only when needed.

semantic_distinctions.label: IPsec vs higher-layer security
semantic_distinctions.description: The source discusses IPsec at the IP layer but does not equate it with TLS; both occupy different architectural positions.

semantic_distinctions.label: Native vs tunneled IPv6
semantic_distinctions.description: Native IPv6 traverses IPv6-capable infrastructure; tunneling carries IPv6 over IPv4 infrastructure.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 is just IPv4 with bigger addresses
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 changes packet format, address architecture, fragmentation behavior, neighbor discovery, multicast/broadcast semantics and other protocol functions.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 supports broadcast
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 does not define traditional broadcast addresses; multicast is used instead.

misconceptions.title: Routers fragment IPv6 packets
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 routers do not fragment; hosts use PMTU discovery or endpoint fragmentation.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 addresses always need DHCP
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 supports SLAAC and hosts generate link-local addresses automatically; DHCPv6 is optional for additional state.

misconceptions.title: Every IPv6 address is globally routable
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 interfaces require link-local addressing and may have multiple address types; global unicast is only one category.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 cannot be scanned
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly notes that configuration patterns can make scanning feasible in real-world scenarios.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 has a header checksum like IPv4
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 omits the base-header checksum.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 and IPv4 interoperate directly
misconceptions.correction: The source states the protocols are not directly interoperable and require transition mechanisms.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 extension headers are always harmless to routers
misconceptions.correction: Some implementations process extension headers in software/CPU paths, causing performance or security issues.

misconceptions.title: Global IPv6 addressing eliminates privacy concerns
misconceptions.correction: Stable globally addressable identifiers can facilitate tracking; temporary addresses mitigate this concern.

misconceptions.title: Tunneling is equivalent to native IPv6
misconceptions.correction: Tunneling adds encapsulation and can reduce MTU/increase latency.

misconceptions.title: NDP is just ARP with a new address format
misconceptions.correction: NDP uses ICMPv6 and multicast and also handles router discovery and address configuration.

misconceptions.title: AAAA records are IPv4 DNS records
misconceptions.correction: AAAA records map names to IPv6 addresses; A records map names to IPv4.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 deployment means IPv4 disappears immediately
misconceptions.correction: The source describes coexistence and transition mechanisms because both protocols operate simultaneously.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 security is automatically stronger because of the larger address space
misconceptions.correction: The source identifies implementation and operational security risks, including shadow networks and fragmentation evasion.
